clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant hereditary spastic paraplegia caused by mutations in NIPA1 on chromosome 15, usually presenting as a pure (uncomplicated) spastic paraparesis.
Onset is typically in adolescence or adult life with slowly progressive lower-limb spasticity, a spastic gait and lower-limb hyperreflexia.
A recurrent missense change (classically a substitution at residue 45) accounts for most families, favouring a dominant-negative or gain-of-function mechanism over simple haploinsufficiency.
Although usually pure, complicated presentations are described with epilepsy, peripheral neuropathy or mild cognitive change.
NIPA1 encodes a magnesium and cation transporter enriched in neurons; mutant protein is retained intracellularly and enhances bone morphogenetic protein signalling in axons.
NIPA1 variants also arise as susceptibility alleles in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, underscoring a shared vulnerability of long motor axons.
Penetrance is generally high but age-dependent; urinary urgency and reduced ankle vibration sense are common accompaniments.
reference.pathophysiology: NIPA1 (non-imprinted in Prader-Willi/Angelman syndrome region 1) encodes an integral membrane magnesium and cation transporter that cycles between the plasma membrane and early endosomes and is highly expressed in neurons, including large projection neurons. Disease-causing mutations, most often affecting a specific extracellular or transmembrane residue, cause misfolding and endoplasmic-reticulum retention of the protein with a dominant effect on the wild-type allele, and lead to enhanced signalling through the bone morphogenetic protein pathway, a pathway repeatedly implicated across hereditary spastic paraplegia subtypes in the control of axonal transport and outgrowth. The consequence is a length-dependent, dying-back degeneration of the distal ends of the longest corticospinal-tract axons and, to a lesser extent, the dorsal columns, giving progressive spasticity with relatively preserved strength. The overlap of NIPA1 variation with motor neuron disease highlights the transporter's role in maintaining the homeostasis of very long axons.
additionalDifferentials: Other autosomal dominant pure hereditary spastic paraplegias (SPG4/SPAST, SPG3A/ATL1, SPG31/REEP1)
Dopa-responsive dystonia mimicking a spastic gait in younger patients
Vitamin B12 or copper deficiency myelopathy
additionalInvestigations: NIPA1 sequencing within a hereditary spastic paraplegia gene panel
MRI brain and whole spine to exclude structural, compressive and demyelinating causes
Nerve conduction studies where neuropathic features are present
Very-long-chain fatty acids and vitamin B12/copper to exclude treatable mimics
Family segregation testing given the dominant inheritance
redFlags: Prominent lower motor neuron or bulbar signs suggesting motor neuron disease
A sensory level, back pain or sphincter loss suggesting compressive myelopathy
Rapid progression over weeks to months
Marked asymmetry or a relapsing course suggesting an inflammatory cause
reference.prognosis: Slowly progressive over decades; most patients retain ambulation, often with walking aids, and life expectancy is typically normal in the pure form.
pitfalls: Attributing a dominant pure hereditary spastic paraplegia to the commonest gene (SPAST) without testing NIPA1
Settling on a genetic label before excluding treatable mimics such as B12/copper deficiency or a compressive myelopathy
Assuming an absent family history excludes a dominant disorder given de novo variants and reduced penetrance
Overlooking the amyotrophic lateral sclerosis overlap when counselling a family about a NIPA1 variant
management: Symptomatic antispasticity therapy with baclofen or tizanidine, escalating to intrathecal baclofen for refractory spasticity, plus botulinum toxin for focal spasticity
Regular physiotherapy, stretching and provision of orthoses and walking aids to maintain gait
Bladder care with urodynamic assessment and antimuscarinic therapy for urinary symptoms
Anti-seizure medication if epilepsy occurs in complicated presentations
Surveillance for gait deterioration, contractures and any complicating neuropathy or cognitive change
Genetic counselling for autosomal dominant inheritance, offering predictive testing to relatives
